Mridul: Back from the village. So glad I went before ordering books.
Bidisha: Tell me. What did they say?
Mridul: Talked to eight parents and three teachers, on the school steps and one evening at the tea stall.
Mridul: Everyone said the same thing: kids can't study after dark. Power cuts, and one bulb at home.
Bidisha: Not more books? 😮
Mridul: Books came third. First lighting, second a quiet room with a table.
Bidisha: So the library becomes a study room with a lamp?
Mridul: Yes 🙂 The panchayat hall is empty in the evenings, and one teacher offered to hold the key.
Bidisha: Then what are you buying first?
Mridul: Two solar lamps and six mats. Books later, when the kids tell me what they want.

qa.q: How many parents and teachers did Mridul talk to?
qa.a: Mridul talked to eight parents and three teachers.

qa.q: How did Mridul feel about going to the village first?
qa.a: Mridul felt glad and relieved to have listened before ordering books, since it changed the whole plan.

qa.q: What could Mridul do next to check the plan works?
qa.a: Mridul could open the room for a week and ask families what changes they notice, since real use shows what to adjust.

qa.q: How might the teacher who offered to hold the key see the plan?
qa.a: The teacher probably feels supportive and hopeful, since offering the key shows trust in the idea.

grounding: Shows a person talking with parents and teachers in a village and learning that evening light and study space matter more than new books.

passage:
Anjali had collected three hundred donated books in her Pune flat for a library in her mother's village near Wardha. Before she hired a tempo, she went to the village for a week with a notebook, not the books.
She sat on verandahs with parents and spent afternoons with Madhuri Tai, the headmistress. She asked one thing again and again: 'What stops the children from studying in the evening?'
Nobody said books. 'Light,' said a mother whose house got power for four hours a day. 'A place,' said Madhuri Tai. 'Five children in one room with the TV on. Where will they sit?'
Anjali went back to Pune and changed the plan. The first step would be a solar-lit room at the school, open from six to nine every evening. The books would come later, a hundred at a time.

qa.q: How many donated books had Anjali collected?
How might Anjali have felt when nobody said books?
qa.a: Anjali was probably surprised and a little deflated at first, then grateful to learn before spending on the wrong thing.

qa.q: Why was going with a notebook instead of the books a wise first step?
qa.a: It let the community say what they needed, so the plan fits real problems like light and space.

qa.q: How might the mother whose house has power four hours a day see the new plan?
qa.a: She'd likely feel heard and relieved, since a lit room gives her children somewhere to study in the evening.

grounding: It shows someone talking with parents and teachers in the village before starting a library and learning that evening light and study space matter more than books.

subtopic: Planning a legacy or purpose project
subtype: Approach: listening to the community before designing [Action]
passage:
Sofia had grown up in Cape Town and wanted to give something back to the small town in the Eastern Cape where her grandmother had taught. Her first idea was a library with new books. But before ordering anything, she spent two weeks there, sitting in on classes and visiting families after school.
Lindiwe, a teacher at the primary school, walked her through the township at dusk. 'Look,' she said. Windows were dark; many homes had no electricity once the prepaid meter ran out. 'The children have books from school. What they don't have is light and a quiet table.'
Sofia rewrote her plan on the drive back. First, a room at the community hall with solar lamps and tables, open every weekday evening, with a volunteer to keep it safe. Books would follow, chosen with the teachers.

qa.a: In a small town in the Eastern Cape.

qa.q: How might Sofia have felt walking with Lindiwe at dusk?
qa.a: Sofia may have felt humbled and a little uneasy, seeing that her first idea didn't match what the children most needed.

qa.q: What else could Sofia do before opening the room?
qa.a: She could check with parents about the best evening hours and safe routes home, so the room fits family life.

qa.q: How might Lindiwe see Sofia's changed plan?
qa.a: Lindiwe would likely feel respected and hopeful, seeing that her observation shaped the plan.

grounding: It shows someone listening to teachers and families before starting a library and learning that evening light and study space matter more than new books.
